planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight water and fertilizer stress. Oo-La-La is a low, wide-spreading cultivar well suited to hanging baskets and cascading over walls.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun. Oo-La-La is a slow-growing, multi-stemmed selection that stays low while spreading wide, producing an extended flush of bright magenta-red bracts over glossy dark green foliage, which makes it a popular choice for cascading over retaining walls, trailing from hanging baskets, or covering a sunny bank as a groundcover. As with other bougainvillea, avoid overwatering and excess nitrogen fertilizer, both of which push leafy growth at the expense of bract production. In zone 9a, give it a sheltered, south-facing site and be prepared to protect it with frost cloth or bring container specimens indoors during hard freeze events, since even brief exposure to temperatures near freezing can cause significant dieback.

common_name: Bengal Orange Bougainvillea (Variegated Vigorous Orange-Bracted Climbing Vine)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight water and fertilizer stress. Bengal Orange is a vigorous, thorny climber best given a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor to cover.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun. Bengal Orange is a vigorous, long-caned climbing bougainvillea with thorny stems and creamy white-variegated foliage that emerges with a coral-pink flush in spring, setting off its vivid pinkish-orange bracts throughout the warm season. Its climbing habit and large mature size make it best suited to covering a sturdy arbor, fence, or wall rather than small container culture. As with other bougainvillea, avoid overwatering and excess nitrogen fertilizer, both of which push leafy growth at the expense of bract production, and site it carefully away from foot traffic given its sharp thorns. In zone 9a, protect young plants with frost cloth during hard freezes, since dieback can occur even though established plants typically resprout from the base.

common_name: Temple Fire Bougainvillea (Dwarf Compact Brick-Red Bougainvillea)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight water and fertilizer stress. Temple Fire is a true dwarf form well suited to small containers and tight landscape spaces.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun. Temple Fire is a true dwarf, multi-stemmed cultivar that stays compact at roughly knee height, bearing dense clusters of brick-red to fuchsia bracts from mid-spring through fall over small, spiny-stemmed growth. Its naturally small stature suits patio containers, hanging baskets, and tight foundation plantings where larger vining types would quickly outgrow the space. As with other bougainvillea, avoid overwatering and excess nitrogen fertilizer, both of which push leafy growth at the expense of bract production. In zone 9a, container-grown plants should be moved to a protected spot or given frost cloth during hard freeze events, since the compact root mass of dwarf cultivars offers less cold buffering than larger, established in-ground plants.
